https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c935.text: Image source, Getty Images By Grace Eliza Goodwin Reporting from New York Published 9 August 2026, 16:19 BST Updated 1 hour ago The operator of a boat that overturned near the Statue of Liberty, killing a woman and a baby, has been arrested and charged with reckless endangerment, New York police said. Officials said a large search and rescue operation was launched after the incident near New York Harbour on Saturday night. A nearby vessel rescued 12 people from the water before police arrived, the US Coast Guard (USCG) said. New York police divers later found a 27-year-old woman and a five-month-old girl, who were transported to a nearby hospital where they later died. The names of passengers and the specific cause of the incident have not been released. Around 22:25 local time (03:25 BST), police received a 911 call reporting an overturned boat in the waters near Liberty Island, which houses the iconic statue. The rescue involved two Coast Guard boats, four fire department boats, two police boats and a police helicopter, the USCG said. The survivors of the incident are all reported to be in stable condition, the agency added. The investigation into the incident is ongoing, officials said. The boat's operator, a 46-year-old Manhattan resident, faces 13 counts of reckless endangerment, officials said. Coast Guard investigators are also determining whether the boat was illegally chartered. An illegal charter is any passenger-for-hire vessel operation that does not have required credentials, safety equipment, and certificate of inspection. "We are extremely grateful for the heroic, swift actions of our partner agencies and Good Samaritan vessel who assisted in rescuing survivors from the water," said Capt Doreen McCarthy of the USCG. https://www.miragenews.com/dna-leads-to-.text: Mirage News Mirage News Mirage News Life 29 Jul 2026 7:04 am AEST Date Time Share Police are renewing their appeal for help to identify the body of a man – also known as 'Echo Point man' – found 22 years ago in the Blue Mountains, after sourcing fresh evidence via DNA technology. About 11.30am on Friday 4 June 2004, emergency services were called to Echo Point, Katoomba, after a report of a body found in bushland. Officers attached to Blue Mountains Police Area Command attended and located the body of a man. Despite extensive inquiries over the past two decades, police have been unable to identify the man; however, fresh information has now been received via advanced DNA analysis. Based on the information received, detectives have now renewed their appeal for information and have released an updated description of the man. The man is believed to be Caucasian, more than 60 years old, about 178cm tall, of medium build, with light grey hair and frontal baldness. Detectives believe the man was also suffering from significant eyesight problems at the time. When the man was found, he was wearing a blue button up shirt, a red cardigan, a cream jacket, blue corduroy pants, a black belt, and brown work boots. Based on recent DNA analysis, detectives have been advised the man's ancestry is likely Latvian. Detectives are now hoping this latest information could lead them to identify the man. Blue Mountains Police Area Command Commander, Superintendent John Nelson, said they hope this additional information could provide leads for his team. "Despite extensive inquiries over many years, this man's identity remains unknown," Superintendent Nelson said. "Since receiving this latest information, we have focused our inquiries in this area but have been unable to identify the man, and we are now appealing to anyone with information about a man missing since early 2000s, possibly with Latvian or Middle European heritage, to contact police. "Police understand this may be a difficult subject, but identifying this man is about dignity, respect, and providing answers to family who may still be searching." Anyone who may have any information is urged to contact investigators attached to Blue Mountains Police Area Command or Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000. Anyone with information about this incident is urged to contact Crime Stoppers: 1800 333 000 or https://nsw.crimestoppers.com.au . Information is treated in strict confidence. The public is reminded not to report information via NSW Police social media pages. /Public Release. Photograph: Marcin Nowak/Anadolu/Getty Images European Union Shabana Mahmood to hold talks with EU over law enforcement cooperation UK home secretary’s meeting comes after PM said he wanted to rejoin European law enforcement databases Lisa O’Carroll senior correspondent Sun 18 Oct 2026 19.13 BST Last modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 19.35 BST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The UK home secretary, Shabana Mahmood , will meet the EU’s home affairs commissioner on Monday for further talks just days after Andy Burnham said he wanted to rejoin European law enforcement databases from which the UK has been locked out of since Brexit. According to the European Commission , they will discuss “migration, border management, law enforcement cooperation and counter-terrorism”, with the latest Frontex data published on Monday showing a 43% decline in small boats crossing the Channel. It will be the second time Mahmood has met Magnus Brunner in two months and comes amid an increase in engagement between London and Brussels since Andy Burnham announced he would use an upcoming EU-UK summit to “ lay out to the country ” what he believes are the “different options for Britain’s long-term relationship” with the EU. Brexit’s back – but are British voters ready to contemplate a reversal? Read more Brunner said “the UK’s contribution is indispensable” to continuing efforts to suppress irregular migration after the EU introduced a suite of new laws aimed at speeding up asylum decisions and deportations. On the agenda for Monday’s meeting will be talks on the UK rejoining some of the police and security databases it was locked out from after Brexit and rejoining a new database, Eurodac , centring on migration. Last week Burnham told MPs that “one of the most positive aspects of my meeting with [the European Commission] president [Ursula] von der Leyen in New York, was her openness to the conversation about restoring data sharing on immigration across the UK, across Europe”. He said it was “control” that the UK “lost” and should get “more attention” in the debate about Brexit . “I will work hard to see if we can get a practical arrangement on that very issue at the summit in November,” Burnham said. View image in fullscreen Magnus Brunner will discuss ‘migration, border management, law enforcement cooperation and counter-terrorism’ with Shabana Mahmood, according to the European Commission. Photograph: Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu/Getty Images Brunner will also meet the MI5 director general, Ken McCallum, and visit the National Counter Terrorism Security Office, as well as meet senior officials from the UK’s child sexual abuse centre to discuss joint efforts to tackle such crimes. He has also been chosen to deliver a lecture at King’s College London on migration and asylum, where he will talk about the impact of the EU’s new Pact on Migration and Asylum, a framework of 10 pieces of legislation overhauling how the EU manages its borders, processes asylum applications and shares information among member states. Brunner will tell those he meets that the new laws have already had a significant impact along with a shift in political priorities around migration in key countries such as Germany, Italy and France. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion He said the “reforms are paying” off in the UK too, with illegal crossings down 43%. “We must stay on this course, including along all relevant migration routes, and the UK’s contribution is indispensable,” he said. “We have put our European house in order. Illegal crossings at our external borders are down 55% over two years, with a further third this year, and asylum applications are at record lows in the countries that used to be main destinations.” One key database the UK wants access to is Eurodac, a new platform which collects fingerprints and facial images of asylum seekers from the age of six, and security flags for people linked to terrorism or serious crime. Another is the Schengen Information System (SIS), which contains data on missing persons, stolen goods, vehicles and number plates, and fugitives crossing internal EU borders. About 20m searches are made daily on the SIS, according to EU data, mostly on cars. The Home Office has not commented.
